The Battle of Stamford Bridge. On the twenty-fifth of September, ten sixty-six, King Harold Godwinson of England defeated an invading Norwegian army led by King Harold Hardrada near the River Derwent in Yorkshire. It was a decisive Saxon victory and also, unknowingly, the last Viking invasion of England. The victory came with tragic consequences.

Harold Hardrada was a legendary warrior—a true Viking king who had sailed the world and earned formidable reputation as one of the most dangerous opponents alive, despite his advanced age. Yet he was killed in this battle, driven by surprise and superior numbers into a rout. The Saxon forces, catching the Norwegians off-guard while they foraged, slaughtered them at the river's edge. It was a complete triumph for the English king.

But the cost was severe. Harold's victory exhausted his forces. The battle's casualties were terrible, and the exhausting three-hundred-mile march north and then back to the south coast left his army depleted and weakened. Just three weeks later, William the Conqueror's Norman army landed on the southern coast of England. Harold's weakened forces, marching from their victory in the north, were unprepared for the Norman invasion that would decide the fate of England. Ironically, the man who had just defeated the last Viking invasion was about to face defeat at the hands of descendants of those very Vikings who had settled Normandy centuries before. Stamford Bridge was Harold's triumph and his undoing.
